items.question: Why do you think formal reasoning has been unapproachable for all but the largest enterprises?
items.object: The cost and accessibility of formal reasoning
items.answer: There's this difficulty where the people who are the experts in the area haven't quite crystallized their view of what should be true, and so we basically go around and around. That loop has been really the expensive part. That's actually why formal reasoning has been unapproachable to all but the largest of enterprises with the most important problems.

That loop has been really the expensive part. That's actually why formal reasoning has been unapproachable to all but the largest of enterprises with the most important problems.

rubrics.text: The response identifies repeated clarification of what domain experts believe should be true as the main source of expense in applying formal reasoning.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between automated reasoning and today’s generative AI?
items.object: The relationship between automated reasoning and generative AI
items.answer:
I think things are kind of shifting around, so when we look back from this time in a couple years, we'll probably be using different names, and actually the ideas will blur. Traditionally, if you look at artificial intelligence, that name was coined in the 1950s. There was this Dartmouth workshop where there were people from cognitive sciences, mathematical logic, Claude Shannon was there, and so on. There was a lot of excitement about the digital computer had come out and was now available to folks, and it was like, “Well, what can we do with this, and how do we make intelligence?” A number of different branches formed out of that. You have symbolic reasoning, cognitive reasoning, and you have theorem proving and these kinds of things.

Then what happened was there was a series of—you know, there was AI winter, various fun pendulum swings on funding. People are excited about it; people think it won't ever be able to do anything; people get really excited about it. These different branches began to lower their ambitions and find niche problems that they could solve. Traditionally, you'd call it symbolic logic or symbolic AI or good old-fashioned AI, these kinds of things. That's the form of reasoning, logical reasoning, and you can write algorithms to automate your reasoning. That's one branch, and it has a lot of commercial impact in proving the correctness of programs. We can talk in a moment about how we're using that and have been using it at Amazon for 10 years.

Meanwhile, the other branches went off to make predictions or identify images and things. What's really happened with the rise of interest in generative AIs is it's really brought the communities back together. You have this idea of neurosymbolic AI, which is basically blurring back what the original folks had in mind, where you combine the cognitive ideas and symbolic ideas together in some sense. The thing that was announced yesterday is a neurosymbolic AI approach, really.

items.question: How do you understand automated reasoning as a way of establishing truths about an intractably large or infinite set?
items.object: Automated reasoning as finite proof over intractably large or infinite domains
items.answer:
Very broadly, I think of reasoning as the art when you're talking about something intractably large or infinite, say, like all possible triangles. That's an uncountable set, so you're not going to be able to enumerate all possible triangles to answer a question about all possible triangles, for example, the Pythagorean theorem. If you have a right-angle triangle, there's a certain thing that holds over all of the right-angle triangles, and that's infinite. You're not going to be able to try them all out.

What you're going to want to do is make a finite argument, an argument in finite space, like a whiteboard or a paper, and time. This interview is an hour, so if we wanted to talk about that in depth, we'd only have an hour. What you're going to want to do is use a well-accepted set of rules. Think like chess: there are only so many rule moves possible, and you're trying to show what's true by finding a series of moves in that game that allows you to go from things that everyone believes are true from the start, those would be the axioms, to the deduction. Reasoning is finding those moves in that rule system to get to an answer. Automated reasoning is merely the algorithmic writing of software to define those proofs.

items.question: What opportunity do you see for applying recent advances in automated reasoning to generative AI?
items.object: Recent automated reasoning breakthroughs and their potential for identifying incorrect generative AI statements
items.answer:
What's pretty amazing is there's been a series of really remarkable breakthroughs over the past 15 years in that space, some really incredible ideas that allow you to solve absolutely enormous problems in those spaces, and to find satisfying assignments in those very complex spaces or to show that there is no satisfying assignment to those rule systems. That's really given rise to a bunch of applications, but they've been largely hidden from customers. We have exposed a couple capabilities to customers, but we didn't really show how those things were working.

The observation that was made when people began getting really excited about generative AI—in particular for me, because I'm in New York City, I started talking to customers about these topics—was the realization that there's a lot we could do in the space of helping customers identify incorrect statements in generative AI.

items.question: How do you understand Amazon’s approach to enabling innovation while addressing security threats?
items.object: Amazon’s approach to security
items.answer: When I first joined Amazon, I actually reported to Steve Schmidt, who is the CISO of all of Amazon now, at the time AWS. The idea was that Amazon—the AWS organization, and now Amazon—has a very unique way of seeing security. The phrase is, “We don't say no; we say, ‘Here's how.’” They're really looking and investing a lot in ways of not shutting teams down when they're trying to do something innovative, but working with them to identify ways to deal with potential threats in the security space when they're trying to build a product. The decision there was to invest in formal verification.

items.question: Why do you see AWS resource policies as a useful application of automated reasoning?
items.object: Automated reasoning about AWS resource policies
items.answer: Very early on, we began to identify stuff we could do, and I worked on five or six things at the start, and all of them have gone extremely well. That is reasoning about AWS policies. It turns out when you're writing systems in AWS, you're identifying configurations of resources and, on the internet, what sorts of principals can touch those resources and take what kinds of actions. Those are expressed as resource policies, and they're very flexible. With flexibility comes—you can write down policies that might not be great. Helping customers understand those policies was one of the first applications of automated reasoning. That shows up nowadays in S3 Block Public Access, IAM Access Analyzer, AWS Config rules. There's a bunch of places. There's an internal thing called Zelkova, which reasons about policies.

items.question: How do you understand the role of learning in making automated reasoning searches tractable?
items.object: Learning and restarts in automated reasoning search
items.answer:
The problems in automated reasoning are typically NP-complete or, if not, undecidable. NP-complete or worse. What that means practically is that the search space has so much branching, and ultimately the problem is: can you find a satisfying assignment? Can you find in this incredibly large tree a node where a certain constraint is met, or can you show that no such one exists? That's the reasoning challenge.

How the tools work is they begin exploring that space somewhat randomly, and then learning lessons that have the effect of pruning away the search space. The analogy I have is, I remember when I was really young, I walked to school, I tripped and fell, and it was because I hadn't tied my shoelaces. From that point on, I check to make sure that my shoes were appropriately tied. But what I didn't do is try all other routes to school. What I did was root-cause what the problem was. That problem of figuring out why you fell has massive branching factors, but you can do a bit of root-causing, figure it out, and then apply that heuristic, and that prunes away the search space. That's kind of how they work: they're enumerating, identifying root causes.

Another example is this idea of restarts. When you're doing a search, the tools often stop the search and just restart from the beginning, but keep the lessons learned. Think about solving a maze: you can go to the end, realize you're at a dead end. If you start from the beginning, you want to capture something about the maze or start from a place where you could have branched differently.

items.question: Why do you regard cache-aligned databases as an important breakthrough for automated reasoning tools?
items.object: Cache-aligned databases in automated reasoning tools
items.answer: One of the really amazing tricks I'd point to was to build the database that maintains those lessons in such a way that aligns well with caches. It turns out there was this paper in 1999 or so. There were professors and postdocs with beautiful algorithms, and then these two undergraduates of Princeton made a tool that in theory was actually worse, because the number of operations that were going to be performed was actually higher. But the performance of the tool was outrageous because it operated on the caches. Suddenly a lot of people began moving to those tools and building on them.

items.question: What excites you about the recent move toward distributed solving in automated reasoning?
items.object: Distributed solving in automated reasoning
items.answer: What's happened recently, something I'm very excited about, is how to distribute solving. The funding model for these tools has always been something like the National Science Foundation funding academics: you'd have a professor, three PhD students, and a postdoc or something like that. It was all work done on a sequential microprocessor. There's an international competition of these tools. For example, the International SAT Competition has been running for 20-some years, and the tools are raced against each other, but only quite recently have the rules allowed distributed or parallel search. Now there's this amazing breakout, because you can imagine if you're allowing a thousand machines to independently search spaces on the same problem and share the lemmas or lessons learned, share the root causes across a network, that could be quite exciting.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for GPU acceleration in automated reasoning solvers?
items.object: GPU acceleration for automated reasoning solvers
items.answer: There are papers. I don't think there's been enough work to really authoritatively say whether or not it—in a bunch of algorithms, there are essentially matrix operations in there, so I would think that we could, but we'll see where stuff lands. There was a blog post two or three years ago that showed that the fastest solver was actually on an iPhone, because the iPhone memory, the speed of the memory on the iPhone, was the best. By basically jailbreaking an iPhone and putting a solver on that, that was actually the fastest solver. There's going to be something to do with what operations you need to make things fast and what you need for planning. We'll see where things net out in the coming years.

items.question: How do you think about the core capabilities of automated reasoning in Bedrock Guardrails?
items.object: Automated reasoning in Bedrock Guardrails
items.answer: Let me say first of all what it is. It's essentially two capabilities. The first capability is an experience involving a subject matter expert in a particular domain, say zoning or electrical codes, where they can define in mathematical logic the set of true and untrue statements in that domain, in a way that they don't need to understand mathematical logic. Then the second capability is the ability to take that formalization and essentially sidecar it next to any other algorithm that's generating statements, or a human that's generating statements, and then the ability to prove or disprove those statements according to the formalization.

items.question: How do you see generative AI changing the accessibility of formal reasoning?
items.object: Generative AI as a way to make formal reasoning more accessible
items.answer: It's really an interesting case where old ideas are great; they're just kind of ahead of their time, and you need some other technology to come in and catalyze that possibility. I think what we're very excited about with generative AI is that it allows us to build capabilities to help people build formalizations in logic. I can't remember exactly when the Transformer paper came out, but when I began to see those models getting bigger and bigger, I was like, “Oh, great, we can use that to help people use the improvers,” which is probably not what most people are thinking. It makes this area that was much less accessible much more accessible, I think.

items.question: How do you see IAM Access Analyzer as a model for helping customers refine policies used to validate LLM responses?
items.object: IAM Access Analyzer as an inspiration for refining policies used to validate LLM responses
items.answer: First of all, I should say this product is going to grow and refine in response to how customers are using it, so we'll see where we land in the future. The big inspiration for us was previous work called IAM Access Analyzer. It's actually a free product for AWS customers. You take your policies, it takes all of the nouns, basically all of the logical constants, I'd say, in logic, and assembles a set of questions, and then asks you whether you think these conditions should be guaranteed. You can say yes or no, and when you say no, it basically has helped you formalize the thing that you want to hold over your policies. As your policies evolve over time, it's able to reestablish the things that you wanted to hold. It helps you figure out what your intent was with your policies.

items.question: How do you think about using a policy's Boolean structure to generate questions that help customers validate it?
items.object: Using Boolean structure to generate questions for policy validation
items.answer: There are a bunch of tricks we can use. For example, when we have a formula that describes truth, the set of true and untrue statements, that has logical structure, Boolean structure, and you can disassemble that Boolean structure. You can take all the convex hulls, or there are various operations you can do over that, and then find satisfying assignments in each of the convex slices of it and ask the customer. It's like a coverage metric. It's saying we explored all the weird corners of this. There may be other values that are sort of neighbors, but you have at least checked all of the representative corners.

items.question: What have you learned about formalizing the rules underlying organizations’ generative AI services?
items.object: Formalizing the rules underlying organizations’ generative AI services
items.answer: The problem was, and you see this a lot in the news, people began deploying those kinds of ideas and then they were misleading their customers. When I looked at it, chatting with customers, I realized that in many cases there were formalizations underneath that, really in their mental model. items.question: How do you think about where automated reasoning is useful, given the difficulty of formalizing law?
items.object: The applicability and limits of formalization and automated reasoning
items.answer: A lot of decisions are just in time. There are different ways of seeing law where the courts will only decide on what the law is based on those just-in-time kind of moments. So it's case law. I do think in some cases you can encode those things, but the bigger point is there's a spectrum. There are certain things which are absolutely clearly formalizable, like mathematics, and then there are things like, “What is a good song?” I think that's going to be very hard to formalize, and then there's a bunch of stuff in the middle. The challenge for us all as a community will be trying to figure out how to help organizations and people figure out when to apply these different tools, and in what order to apply these different tools. There's going to be a bunch of applications for which this capability isn't probably the right thing.

items.answer: First of all, hallucination is good. We like it, right? Hallucination is the creativity. There are a bunch of ways you can say things that just aren't true, don't add up, or won't pass muster.

items.question: How do you think organizations should handle ambiguity in the policies they build with Automated Reasoning Checks?
items.object: Ambiguity and policy maintenance in Automated Reasoning Checks
items.answer: There are a couple of areas where there are ambiguities that we're always going to be navigating. One is the decision on what is true. It may be that the organization has incorrectly encoded what is true; actually, there's a bug in the specification. That's always going to be true. I think what we're going to need to do in the future is make that feedback cycle really easy for your constituents when they find things that they believe are wrong, to help the organization understand that that's wrong and fix it. The second thing is that policies change over time, and so to make it really easy for organizations to make proposed changes and understand the consequence of those changes.

items.question: Why have you found formal reasoning difficult for organizations to adopt?
items.object: The cost and accessibility of formal reasoning
items.answer:
I've worked in biological systems, reasoning about genetic regulatory pathways; I've reasoned about operating systems, device drivers, microprocessors, railway switching systems, aerospace systems, networking policy. What I have found over and over and over and over and over again is this difficulty where the people who are the experts in the area haven't quite crystallized their view of what should be true. So when an organization decides, “This is really important to us to get right. We're going to use formal reasoning,” great, we'll hire a bunch of people like Byron. Then Byron says to a person in that domain, “Okay, explain what should hold,” and they have some ideas and write some stuff on the whiteboard. Then you go and formalize that, and then you go to the system and find a bunch of bugs. You show them the bugs; they're like, “Oh, those aren't really bugs, because we—” And I was like, “Well, you actually did—it's what you said, but okay.” So we basically go around and around, and that loop has been really the expensive part. That's actually why formal reasoning has been unapproachable to all but the largest of enterprises with the most important problems.

If you look at my resume, I've gone from a large organization with big business problems to the next one to the next one, because they could afford it and it was so important to get these things right. What has always happened in these places is that, ultimately, in those teams, the people who become the experts in all the hard corner cases are formal reasoning people. Today that's true in Amazon, in the networking team and the identity team.

items.question: How do you understand the technical difficulty behind Automated Reasoning Checks, given that translating documents into rules and checking responses against a solver sounds straightforward?
items.object: The computational difficulty and growing power of automated reasoning tools
items.answer:
That is, okay, well, you took a document, you asked an LLM to transform that document into some set of rules, there are rules, and you stuck them in a rule solver. When you get back a response, you're checking it against this rule solver. Sounds easy. Well, you are combining multiple tools to solve NP-complete or more problems. One of the interesting things about automated reasoning tools is that, because they are solving NP-complete or undecidable problems, they can go to lunch. The program termination problem is undecidable. In the past I've worked on program termination proofs. We can take a device driver and attempt to prove or disprove termination, but because the problem is undecidable, that tool that's doing that analysis may just run forever. The same is true for NP-complete problems. Propositional satisfiability is NP-complete. It's very easy to find examples and give them to a solver, and that solver will not be able to solve them.

There are open conjectures. For example, Marijn Heule has a translation of the Collatz conjecture directly to problems in propositional logic and the propositional logic solvers. It's a very small problem. It's a small loop: while n is greater than one, if n is divisible by two, divide it by two, and if not, n gets 3n plus 1. You can write it in Python in about three lines of code, and no one knows if that program guarantees termination or not. It's been open since the 1920s, I think, 1910s or 20s. There are a bunch of those open challenges.

Under the hood, what we've been doing in automated reasoning is making these tools more and more powerful, and along the way we've been mopping up a bunch of open math conjectures with the same tool. Ryan has just proved—the formalization will evade me, so don't ask me one more question about it—it's called the Happy Ending problem. That can be reduced, and he's also done the Pythagorean shapes problem. There are a bunch of problems that he's solved using these tools. He's a professor at Carnegie Mellon, but also within Amazon, and in his spare time has been using these same tools to prove those open math conjectures.

items.question: Why do you find research connected to Amazon customers more productive than research in an environment protected from corporate pressures?
items.object: Customer-connected research at Amazon
items.answer:
One of the neat things about being at Amazon is a little counterintuitive. I spent many years in total blue skies, protected from all stress and all corporate realities environments, and I found that doing research in those environments was more challenging than doing it in Amazon, where we're really connected to customers. The reason is that the problems are intractable.

There's this great quote that the division between theory and practice is injurious to computing. Essentially theoreticians don't know what problems to work on. The challenge is, I'm facing undecidable problems, meaning you're going to have to come up with algorithms that either over- or under-approximate solutions to the problem. You're going to have to make decisions about what approximations you're comfortable with and which ones you're uncomfortable with. How are you going to do that? You're going to have to understand the customer problem.

Amazon has a bunch of mechanisms to get really connected to the customers and to let customer problems drive scientific innovation. We're facing a bunch of NP-complete, if not undecidable, problems here, and we're making tools that over-approximate solutions to the problems and helping customers use them. The frontier problems that customers have will drive the innovation, and that's how this capability will improve forever.

items.question: How do you see automated reasoning becoming more closely integrated with the way generative AI chooses tokens?
items.object: Combining automated reasoning with generative AI through constrained decoding and backtracking
items.answer:
There's an area, I think they're calling it constrained decoding, where you're combining these techniques a bit more. You can imagine having a grammar, and then when you're choosing your next token, you can use the grammar to make that set of possible tokens smaller. That's an area where people are beginning to blur these things together more.

Then there's questions around—so a big thing that we do in reasoning is backtracking. When you're choosing tokens, can you backtrack? Maybe you would make multiple versions, let them explore a little bit, and then realize certain decisions were wrong and kill some of those. What would the architecture look like for that? That's an area I see both within Amazon and in the literature people playing around with. That's sort of on the scientific frontier.

On the frontier, what I'm excited to do, and why re:Invent has been so great so far, is we're talking to customers who are now looking at how to use this capability, and lots of these questions are coming up. We'll see where the science goes from there.

items.question: Why do you see generative AI as a promising tool for advancing program verification?
items.object: Generative AI's role in program verification
items.answer:
I'll just make some scientific observations. What we're doing here is looking at natural language and interacting with people who probably don't understand logic, interfacing with systems that are mechanized by people who probably don't understand logic. That's the challenge we're facing there.

If you look at a lot of the applications of what we've done in Amazon, we're talking about code, which is a materially different situation. It's very structured. Code is structured data, in a sense. A program represents all of the infinite, all of the typical infinite set of executions that are possible for that program. It's a representation of the state, and then you have properties you want to prove of programs, and this can be expressed in temporal logic, CTL, LTL, you name it. Then you have distributed systems and concurrent systems, and so on. There's a whole bunch of techniques, and there are applications of generative AI to help make those tools much more accessible.

When you're doing a proof of a program, you're trying to find an inductive invariant, or you're trying to find a ranking function to explain termination. One of the tricks we can use is to ask Transformer-based models to help us find most likely arguments for correctness and then check those. If I look at the scientific literature, it's very clear to me that in the future we'll be merging techniques from generative AI together with program verification to help remove certain kinds of bugs from programs. Figuring out what kinds of bugs you want to remove is something generative AI can help out with, too.

It's super exciting. In the literature, say 10 or 15 years ago, there were papers saying, “When you're reasoning about a program, you're trying to find an inductive invariant. Can we use machine learning to do that?” The techniques weren't that great, but with the commercial investment into building these incredible large language models, it allows us now to do that. Mathematical systems and a program are not that far apart. When you encode a problem into mathematics for doing reasoning, you are essentially encoding it as a computer program. The same techniques you're seeing for people who are solving math conjectures also apply for reasoning about programs. That's very exciting.
